title: Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
learningObjective: Solve application problems using exponential and logarithmic equations.

faqs.question: What makes a word problem an "exponential" or "logarithmic" application?
faqs.answer: Look for a quantity that changes by a constant PERCENT or FACTOR over equal time intervals, rather than by a constant amount. Phrases like "grows by 5% per year," "doubles every 3 hours," "decays at a continuous rate of 17%," or "compounded monthly" are all signals that you're dealing with exponential change — the same constant-ratio idea from EL1, just embedded in a real context.

faqs.question: What is Newton's Law of Cooling, and what does each part of the formula represent?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise). Newton's Law of Cooling models how an object's temperature changes over time as it adjusts toward the temperature of its surroundings.
Formula

\[ T(x) = ab^x + d \]

\( a \) is the difference between the starting temperature and the surrounding temperature, \( b \) is the decay factor, \( x \) is elapsed time, and \( d \) is the surrounding (ambient) temperature — which is also the model's horizontal asymptote.

The coffee cools quickly at first, then levels off as it approaches room temperature — never quite reaching it.

The horizontal asymptote is the room temperature: the \( +d \) moves the asymptote from \( 0 \) up to \( d \) (EL2’s vertical shift), so in the model the temperature levels off at \( d \) but never reaches it. To find when the object reaches a target temperature, subtract \( d \) first, then divide by \( a \) and use logs.

Worked Example

Using \( T(x)=70(0.80)^x+20 \), when does the coffee reach 35°C?

\( 35=70(0.80)^x+20 \) → \( 15=70(0.80)^x \) → \( \tfrac{15}{70}=\tfrac{3}{14}=0.80^x \)

\( x=\dfrac{\log(3/14)}{\log(0.80)}\approx 6.9 \) minutes

faqs.question: What is the compound interest formula, and what does each variable represent?
faqs.answer:
The compound interest formula models an account balance that earns interest at regular intervals throughout the year.
Formula

\[ A(t) = P\left(1+\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} \]

\( A(t) \) is the account value after \( t \) years, \( P \) is the principal (starting amount), \( r \) is the annual interest rate as a decimal, and \( n \) is the number of times interest compounds per year.

Use \( n=1 \) annually, \( n=2 \) semiannually, \( n=4 \) quarterly, \( n=12 \) monthly. Write the rate as a decimal (4% is \( 0.04 \)). CheckIt asks you to round amounts to the nearest dollar.

faqs.question: What is continuous growth/decay, and how is it different from periodic compounding?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise). Continuous growth or decay assumes a quantity is changing constantly, at every single instant, rather than at set intervals (yearly, monthly, etc.) — it's the limiting case of compounding more and more frequently, all the way down to continuously. It is usually written with base \( e \), since \( e \) is the constant that comes out of that continuous-compounding limit (EL1). The base alone doesn't decide it: any model \( ab^t \) can be rewritten as \( ae^{(\ln b)t} \). What matters is what the problem says the rate means: applied once per period (compounded annually, monthly, ...) or at every instant (compounded continuously, a continuous rate).
Formulas

General continuous growth/decay: \( A(t) = ae^{rt} \)

Continuous compounding (finance): \( A(t) = Pe^{rt} \)

faqs.question: How do I know whether an application involves growth or decay?
faqs.answer: Check the sign of the rate or the size of the factor. With a positive starting amount \( a \): for \( A(t)=ae^{rt} \), if \( r>0 \) it's growth and if \( r<0 \) it's decay. For \( f(x)=ab^x \), if \( b>1 \) it's growth and if \( 0<b<1 \) it's decay, the same rule from EL1. In CheckIt's depreciation model the factor is \( 1-r \), and in the half-life model it is \( \tfrac12 \) per half-life, so both are decay. (CheckIt calls \( b \) the “growth rate,” but it is the factor you multiply by each period.)

faqs.question: How do I build an exponential model from a word problem when I'm given a starting value and one other data point?
faqs.answer:
The starting value IS your \( a \). Plug the other data point into \( N(t)=ab^t \) along with that \( a \), then solve algebraically for \( b \).
Worked Example

In 2006, 80 deer were introduced. By 2012 (6 years later), the population reached 180.

Initial value: \( a=80 \)

Plug in: \( 180=80b^6 \) → \( b^6=2.25 \) → \( b=2.25^{1/6}\approx 1.1447 \)

Model: \( N(t)=80(1.1447)^t \)

faqs.question: How do I build an exponential model from a word problem when I'm given two data points, neither at time zero?
faqs.answer: Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise). Use the exact same method from EL1 for finding an equation from two points: divide the two output values to find the common ratio over however many steps apart they are, take the appropriate root to find \( b \), then work backward (or forward) to find \( a \).

faqs.question: How do I use the compound interest formula to find the value of an account after a given number of years?
faqs.answer:
Identify \( P \), \( r \), and \( n \) from the problem, plug them in along with the given \( t \), and evaluate.
Worked Example

$5,000 invested at 4% annual interest, compounded quarterly, for 10 years.

\( P=5000, r=0.04, n=4, t=10 \)

\( A(10) = 5000\left(1+\dfrac{0.04}{4}\right)^{4(10)} = 5000(1.01)^{40} \approx \$7{,}444.32 \), or $7,444 to the nearest dollar, the way CheckIt rounds.

faqs.question: How do I use the continuous compounding/growth formula, and when do I use it instead of the periodic formula?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise). Use the continuous formula \( A(t)=Pe^{rt} \) only when a problem says “compounded continuously” or gives a continuous rate. Otherwise use the model the problem gives you: the periodic compound interest formula with the stated \( n \), \( a\cdot b^t \) for a population, \( A(1-r)^t \) for depreciation, or \( A\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h} \) for half-life. The EL7 CheckIt problems always give you one of those four models, never base \( e \).
Worked Example

$1,000 invested at 10% compounded continuously for 1 year.

\( A(1)=1000e^{0.10(1)} \approx \$1{,}105.17 \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an application problem for time, like "when will this population reach a certain size?"
faqs.answer:
Set the model equal to the target value, then solve for \( t \) using logarithms — exactly the EL6 equation-solving method, just with meaning attached to every variable. (ln or log both work, as long as you use the same one on both sides.)
Worked Example

Using the deer model \( N(t)=80(1.1447)^t \) built in the FAQ above, when does the population reach 250?

\( 250 = 80(1.1447)^t \) → \( 3.125 = 1.1447^t \)

Take log of both sides: \( t = \dfrac{\log(3.125)}{\log(1.1447)} \approx 8.43 \) years

faqs.question: How do I set up and solve a depreciation problem?
faqs.answer: A value that loses a fixed percent each year keeps the rest: losing \( r \) (as a decimal) leaves the factor \( 1-r \), so \( A(t)=A(1-r)^t \). Losing 5% a year keeps 95%, factor \( 0.95 \), not \( 1.05 \) or \( 0.05 \). To find a value, plug in \( t \). To find a time, divide by the starting value, then use logs: \( t=\dfrac{\ln(\text{target}/A)}{\ln(1-r)} \). Both logs are negative, so the time is positive.

faqs.question: How do I solve a half-life problem?
faqs.answer: Use \( A(t)=A\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h} \): the exponent \( \tfrac{t}{h} \) counts half-lives. If \( t \) is a whole number of half-lives, just halve that many times. If the remaining fraction is not an exact power of \( \tfrac12 \) (CheckIt rounds amounts to whole numbers, so this happens often), divide by the starting amount and use logs: \( t=h\cdot\dfrac{\ln(\text{amount}/A)}{\ln(1/2)} \).

faqs.question: How should I round my EL7 answers?
faqs.answer: Keep full calculator precision until the last step. CheckIt gives amounts as whole numbers (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts it shows you are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one, so round your final answer as the problem asks.

faqs.question: How do I set up and solve a continuous decay problem, like radioactive decay?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise). Use \( A(t)=ae^{rt} \) with a NEGATIVE rate \( r \) when a problem gives a continuous decay rate, plug in the given information, and solve for whatever is missing with the same log-based method. (EL7 CheckIt half-life problems use \( A(t)=A\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h} \) instead; see the half-life FAQ above.)
Worked Example

A radioactive substance decays continuously at 17.3% per day. How much of a 100 mg sample remains after 3 days?

\( A(t)=100e^{-0.173t} \)

\( A(3)=100e^{-0.173(3)}=100e^{-0.519} \approx 59.51 \) mg

faqs.question: How does everything from EL1–EL6 come together in this section?
faqs.answer: This section is the payoff for the entire chapter. EL1 gave you the exponential model and how to build one from data. EL2 gave you the asymptote and shift behavior that explains Newton's Law of Cooling's leveling-off shape. EL3 and EL4 gave you logarithms and their graphs. EL5 gave you the properties needed to manipulate these equations. EL6 gave you the actual technique — taking logs of both sides — for solving for a variable trapped in an exponent. Every single piece from this chapter shows up somewhere in a real application here.

faqs.question: Why do these application skills matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Exponential and logarithmic models are how professionals in finance, biology, chemistry, medicine, and public policy actually describe and predict real change — compound interest projections, drug dosage decay in the bloodstream, population and epidemic modeling, and radiometric dating all rely on exactly the skills built in this chapter. Being able to build a model from real data and then solve it for a specific target is one of the most directly applicable skills in this entire course.

guided.title: Practice Building a Population Model
guided.prompt:
I'm a Math 172 student practicing EL7 population problems. Give me one problem: a population of bacteria, deer, algae, or jellyfish grows by P(t) = a * b^t. Tell me the starting population a and the population after k time units, where k is 2, 3, 4, or 5. Build the numbers from a growth factor b between 1.2 and 3.5 with one decimal place (like 1.4 or 2.3), and round the later population to a whole number. Don't tell me b.
1. Ask me to find b. Wait for my work. If I'm stuck, ask me what to divide by and which root to take instead of telling me. If my b comes out like 1.39998, remind me that the later population was rounded.
2. Ask me how many there will be after a later whole number of time units (up to 10), rounded to a whole number. Then pick a whole-number target and ask how long until the population reaches it. Wait for my work each time.
3. Then solve a new problem of the same kind yourself, showing every step, with exactly one deliberate mistake: either divide the later population by the starting population and call that b (forgetting the root), or take the root of the later population without dividing by the starting population first. Don't tell me which.
4. I'll find the mistake and explain why it is wrong.
After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice the Compound Interest Formula
guided.prompt:
I'm a Math 172 student practicing EL7 compound interest with A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Give me one problem: a starting amount between $10,000 and $30,000, an annual rate between 2% and 6%, compounded annually, semiannually, quarterly, or monthly (monthly means n = 12).
1. Ask me to write the model with the numbers in it, then find the amount after a whole number of years between 5 and 25, rounded to the nearest dollar. Wait for my work. If I slip, ask a guiding question instead of giving the answer.
2. Then pick a different whole number of years, work out the amount at that time yourself, round it to the nearest dollar, and ask me how long it takes to reach that amount. My answer should come out very close to a whole number of years.
3. Then solve one more time question yourself, showing every step, with exactly one deliberate mistake: either write the rate as a whole number (for example 4 instead of 0.04), or raise the starting amount to the power along with the base (for example rewriting 20000(1.01)^(4t) as 20200^(4t)). Don't tell me which.
4. I'll find the mistake and say what the correct step is.
After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Practice Newton's Law of Cooling
guided.prompt:
This is an Extension, beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise. I'm practicing Newton's Law of Cooling in the form T(x) = a * b^x + d, where d is the room temperature, a is the starting temperature minus the room temperature, and b is between 0 and 1. Give me a hot drink cooling in a room: a starting temperature, a room temperature that is above 0 degrees and below the starting temperature, and a value of b.
1. Ask me to write the model and find the temperature after a given number of minutes. Wait for my work.
2. Then give me a target temperature strictly between the room temperature and the starting temperature, and ask how long it takes to reach it. Wait for my work, and ask guiding questions instead of giving answers.
3. Then solve one more time question yourself with exactly one deliberate mistake: either forget to subtract the room temperature (solving a * b^x = target), or divide by the starting temperature instead of by a. Don't tell me which.
4. I'll find the mistake, and I'll also explain why a target at or below the room temperature would have no solution.
After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Periodic vs. Continuous Growth
guided.prompt:
This is an Extension, beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise. Give me six short scenarios, one at a time. Include at least two that say “compounded annually,” “semiannually,” “quarterly,” or “monthly”; at least one that says “compounded continuously” or gives “a continuous rate”; one that says an item “loses p% of its value each year”; one that gives a half-life; and one that gives a population at the start and after a few days. For each, ask me which model fits: P(1 + r/n)^(nt) (and what n is), P e^(rt), A(1 - r)^t, A(1/2)^(t/h), or a * b^t, and why. Don't tell me the answer before I commit. After all six, give me your own answer key with exactly one deliberate mistake: match one of the periodic-compounding scenarios to P e^(rt). Don't tell me which one.
I'll find the mistake and explain how the wording tells you the right model.
After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Connect the Whole EL Chapter to One Application
guided.prompt:
I'm a Math 172 student. These are the sections of our exponential and logarithm chapter: EL1 Introduction to Exponentials (exponential models, finding an equation), EL2 Graphs of Exponential Functions (asymptotes), EL3 Introduction to Logarithms (switching between exponential and log form; ln and log), EL4 Graphs of Logarithmic Functions, EL5 Properties of Logarithms, EL6 Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations.
Give me one population problem with P(t) = a * b^t: a starting count, the count after 3 days, a question about the count after a later number of days, and a question about when the count reaches a target. Don't solve it.
1. I'll solve it step by step. After each step I'll name the section the step comes from. Ask me why, and push back if my reason is vague, but don't give me the answer.
2. When I'm done, write your own full solution with a section label on every step. Make exactly one deliberate math mistake in one step: either use the later count divided by the starting count (that is b^3) as if it were b, or multiply the starting count into the base before taking logs (for example rewriting 3000(1.4)^t as 4200^t). Don't tell me which.
3. I'll find the mistake and also check each of your section labels against the list above.
After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: EL7: Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
paths.sectionLabel: EL7, Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the EL7 check: compound interest, population growth, depreciation, and half-life, finding an amount at a given time and the time for a given amount. Practice scope: the four EL7 CheckIt situations; anything using continuous growth (base e) is marked Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise).

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL7 leans on: percents as growth factors and solving exponential equations (EL6). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Percents and growth factors
stops.target: Change a percent to a decimal (\(5.25\% = 0.0525\)). Growth by \(r\) means multiplying by \(1 + r\); decay by \(r\) means multiplying by \(1 - r\) (with \(r\) written as a decimal). For compounding, the rate per period is \(\tfrac{r}{n}\).
stops.cold: (a) Write \(3.25\%\) as a decimal. (b) What is the growth factor for 4% growth per year? (c) For 3.25% compounded quarterly, what is \(\tfrac{r}{n}\)?
stops.coldPlain: (a) Write 3.25% as a decimal. (b) Growth factor for 4% growth per year? (c) For 3.25% compounded quarterly, what is r/n?
stops.solution: Move the decimal two places left: 3.25% = 0.0325. Growing by 4% keeps 100% and adds 4%: factor 1.04. Quarterly means n = 4: 0.0325/4 = 0.008125.
stops.mistake: Using 3.25 instead of 0.0325, or 1.4 instead of 1.04.
stops.again: (a) A car loses 5.5% of its value each year. What is the yearly factor? (b) For 6% compounded monthly, what are \(n\) and \(\tfrac{r}{n}\)?
stops.reflect: How do you tell whether to use \(1 + r\) or \(1 - r\)?

stops.title: Solve for an exponent
stops.target: Recall from EL6: isolate the power, then use logs. For \(b > 0\), \(b \ne 1\) and \(c > 0\), \(b^t = c\) gives \(t = \dfrac{\ln c}{\ln b}\).
stops.cold: Solve \(1.05^t = 2\). Round to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: Solve 1.05^t = 2. Round to four decimal places.
stops.solution: Take ln of both sides: t ln 1.05 = ln 2, so t = ln 2 / ln 1.05, about 14.2067.
stops.reflect: What do you always do before taking a log?

stages.desc: Every EL7 scenario asks two kinds of question: given the time, find the amount (evaluate), or given the amount, find the time (solve with logs). One stop per scenario type on the check.

stops.title: Compound interest
stops.target: Use \(A(t) = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\). To find the amount, plug in \(t\). To find the time, plug in \(A\), isolate the power, and use logs.
stops.cold: A savings account starts with $22,000 and earns 5% compounded quarterly. (a) How much will be in the account after 6 years? Round to the nearest dollar. (b) How long will it take for the account to have $46,358?
stops.coldPlain: A savings account starts with $22,000 and earns 5% compounded quarterly. (a) How much after 6 years, to the nearest dollar? (b) How long until it has $46,358?
stops.mistake: Using n instead of nt in the exponent, or forgetting to divide by P before taking logs.
stops.again: $16,000 at 3% compounded monthly. (a) How much after 8 years? Round to the nearest dollar. (b) How long until it has $22,923?
stops.stretch: Extension (beyond the EL7 CheckIt exercise): If the same $16,000 earned 3% compounded continuously, \(A = Pe^{rt}\), how much would it be after 8 years?
stops.stretchA: \(16{,}000e^{0.03(8)} = 16{,}000e^{0.24} \approx 20{,}339.99\), about $20,340: $6 more than monthly compounding (that is \(e\) from EL1).
stops.reflect: Which question uses logs, and why?
stops.note: CheckIt rounds amounts to the nearest whole number (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one: keep full calculator precision until the last step, then round as the problem asks.

stops.title: Population growth
stops.target: For \(P(t) = a \cdot b^t\): \(a\) is the starting population and \(b\) is the growth factor (CheckIt calls it the “growth rate”). If you are told the population at a later time, use it to find \(b\) first: divide by \(a\), then take a root. Then answer the questions.
stops.cold: A colony starts with 3,000 bacteria; after 3 days there are 8,232. (a) Find \(b\). (b) How many bacteria will there be after 7 days? (c) How long will it take for there to be 61,983 bacteria?
stops.coldPlain: A colony starts with 3,000 bacteria; after 3 days there are 8,232. (a) Find b. (b) How many after 7 days? (c) How long until there are 61,983?
stops.solution: (a) Plug in the known point: 3000 b^3 = 8232, so b^3 = 2.744 and b = cube root of 2.744 = 1.4. (b) P(7) = 3000(1.4)^7, about 31,624.05, so about 31,624 bacteria. (c) 3000(1.4)^t = 61983 gives 1.4^t = 20.661, so t = ln 20.661 / ln 1.4, about 9.00 days.
stops.mistake: Finding b by dividing 8,232 by 3,000 (that gives b^3, not b), or dividing 2.744 by 3 instead of taking the cube root.
stops.again: 300 deer grow to 4,800 after 4 years. Find \(b\), the population after 6 years, and how long until there are 38,400 deer.
stops.reflect: Why do you need a root to find \(b\)?
stops.note: CheckIt rounds amounts to the nearest whole number (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one: keep full calculator precision until the last step, then round as the problem asks.

stops.title: Depreciation
stops.target: A value that loses a fixed percent \(r\) of its value each year (\(r\) as a decimal) follows \(A(t) = A(1 - r)^t\), where the \(A\) on the right is the starting value. The factor \(1 - r\) is between 0 and 1, so the value decreases toward 0 but never reaches it.
stops.cold: A car is worth $36,000 and depreciates 4.5% per year. (a) How much will it be worth after 7 years? (b) After how long will it be worth $18,045?
stops.coldPlain: A car is worth $36,000 and depreciates 4.5% per year. (a) Value after 7 years? (b) After how long will it be worth $18,045?
stops.solution: Losing 4.5% keeps 95.5%: factor 1 - 0.045 = 0.955. (a) 36000(0.955)^7, about 26,081.11, so about $26,081. (b) Divide by 36000: 0.955^t = 0.50125, so t = ln 0.50125 / ln 0.955, about 15.00 years. Both logs are negative (about -0.6907 and -0.0460), so the time comes out positive.
stops.again: A boat worth $55,000 depreciates 3.5% per year. How much will it be worth after 10 years? After how long will it be worth $34,611?
stops.reflect: Why does dividing one negative logarithm by another give a positive time?
stops.note: CheckIt rounds amounts to the nearest whole number (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one: keep full calculator precision until the last step, then round as the problem asks.

stops.title: Half-life
stops.target: For radioactive decay, \(A(t) = A_0\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/h}\), where \(A_0\) is the starting amount (CheckIt writes it as \(A\)) and \(h\) is the half-life: every \(h\) units of time, the amount present is cut in half.
stops.cold: Uranium-235 has a half-life of 704 million years. A sample has 640 grams. (a) How much will be left after 2,112 million years? (b) After how long will there be 20 grams left?
stops.coldPlain: Uranium-235 has a half-life of 704 million years. A sample has 640 grams. (a) How much after 2,112 million years? (b) When will 20 grams be left?
stops.coldA:
\(A(t) = 640\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/704}\), with \(t\) in millions of years.
(a) \(\tfrac{2{,}112}{704} = 3\) half-lives: \(640 \cdot \tfrac{1}{8} = 80\) grams.
(b) \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/704} = \tfrac{20}{640} = \tfrac{1}{32}\), so \(\tfrac{t}{704} = 5\) and \(t = 3{,}520\) million years.[[graph:HL]]
stops.solution: (a) t/704 = 2112/704 = 3, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 and 640/8 = 80 grams. (b) Divide by 640: (1/2)^(t/704) = 1/32 = (1/2)^5, so t/704 = 5 and t = 3,520 million years. When the fraction is not exactly a power of 1/2, use logs: t = h ln(A/A_0) / ln(1/2).
stops.mistake: Multiplying 2,112 by 1/2 instead of counting half-lives (2,112 ÷ 704 = 3), or writing the exponent as 704t.
stops.again: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A sample has 160 grams. How much will be left after 11,460 years? After how long will there be 5 grams left?
stops.stretch: CheckIt rounds amounts to whole numbers, so the amount you are given may not be an exact power of \(\tfrac12\) of the start. A cesium-137 sample (half-life 30 years) starts with 300 micrograms. After how long will there be 9 micrograms left? Round to the nearest year.
stops.stretchA: \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/30} = \tfrac{9}{300} = 0.03\). That is not a power of \(\tfrac12\), so use logs: \(\tfrac{t}{30} = \dfrac{\ln 0.03}{\ln 0.5} \approx 5.059\), so \(t \approx 152\) years. Five half-lives (150 years) would leave 9.375 micrograms, which rounds to 9.
stops.reflect: How can you sometimes solve a half-life problem without logs?
stops.note: CheckIt rounds amounts to the nearest whole number (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one: keep full calculator precision until the last step, then round as the problem asks.

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the EL7 CheckIt: one scenario, one "find the amount" and one "find the time" question. CheckIt may ask them in either order.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Set up the model, then evaluate it for a given time and solve it for a given amount.
stops.cold:
A certificate of deposit has $25,000 in it initially. It earns interest at a rate of 4.5%, compounded semiannually, modeled by \(A(t) = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\).
(a) How much will be in the account after 12 years? Round to the nearest dollar.
(b) How long will it take for the account to have $50,953?
stops.coldPlain: A CD has $25,000 initially at 4.5% compounded semiannually, A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). (a) Amount after 12 years, to the nearest dollar? (b) How long until $50,953?
stops.mistake: Using n = 1 for semiannual (it is 2), or not dividing by P first.
stops.again:
Three more CheckIt-style problems, one for each of the other situations.
Population. Algae grow exponentially, \(P(t) = a \cdot b^t\). There are 3,000 initially and 17,280 after 2 days. (a) How long will it take for there to be 7,925,423 algae? (b) How many algae will there be after 6 days?
Depreciation. An RV is initially valued at $48,000 and depreciates at a rate of 2.75% each year, modeled by \(A(t) = A(1 - r)^t\). (c) How much will the RV be worth after 9 years? (d) After how long will the RV be worth $26,725?
Half-life. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,065 years. A scientist has a sample of 720 grams, which decays according to \(A(t) = A\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/h}\). (e) After how long will there be 45 grams left? (f) How much will be left after 48,130 years?
stops.reflect: How do you know which question needs logs?
stops.note: CheckIt rounds amounts to the nearest whole number (the nearest dollar for money), and its answer key gives times as whole numbers. Because the amounts are rounded, your time will usually come out close to a whole number, not exactly on one: keep full calculator precision until the last step, then round as the problem asks.
